259.t: Playing around Franklin and Iberville and the dog house
259.s: He played in the French Quarter district, the dog house and other spots around Franklin and Iberville, until about seven or eight years earlier.
259.q: Iberville. Oh yeah, yeah. John 25, there was a place around there, Pete Lally, Howard Parker, Billy, you know, all of them, but the district was open. And then that's the district closed where everything was like, but I used to play around in the French Quarter, you know, that part in the doghouse.…

259.t: Band at the Tuxedo and the 25, and clubs like Rice's
259.s: He worked with John Kazman and a small unnamed band (Alcee, T-Ball, Albert Fernandez), and talks of Rice's and the Entertainers clubs.
259.q: So who did you work with in the district? What bands? John Kazman. Then I worked with that team at the doghouse for about three years and a half.

763.t: Honeysuckle Inn, other clubs and Timberline district
763.s: He explains the Honeysuckle Inn's location near West End, plays with Sharkey there, and lists clubs he played, avoiding the Tenderloin.
763.q: Um... Valley Dufour. Oh, yeah. If I could think, if I want to get a chance to think of it like that, you know, it takes time. Yeah. It's so long, you know what I mean? Yeah. Now they talk about a good sax man. That's Zach Valley Dufour. He's a good clarinetist too, I've heard of. That's how I'm…

763.t: Freddie Newman and the Silver Slipper club
763.s: Freddie Newman was his piano player at the Ringside, and he recalls the Italian-owned nightclub on Bienville Street.
763.q: Oh, I played with Freddie Newman plenty of times. I played with Freddie Newman. Freddie Newman was our piano player when we played at the ringside for Pete Whippen. And then when we played for, what is his name, I can't think of his name, he had a nightclub on Bienville Street.

174.t: San Jacinto Club and keno games
174.s: Dejan belonged only to his father's San Jacinto Club, remembers its matinees, boxing and keno, and playing with Manuel Perez.
174.q: No, no, no, no, no, no they don't have, I don't think they have no club. The hall is running, you know, for dance and so forth and so on.

859.t: The Alley club by St. Bernard market
859.s: Interviewer asks about the Alley: a single small hole-in-the-wall club where Rene's band played.
859.ch: Louis Dumaine and Kid Rene bands
859.q: It was a little hole in the wall, a little night club, you know, and they would play down there.

247.t: Boston and Pickwick clubs, Bucktown and Tranchina's
247.s: The interviewer asks where he played; he names the Boston and Pickwick clubs, the Bucktown location near the lake and Tranchina's.
247.q: And Boston Club and Pickwick Club. What's the bass player name? The bass player name is bass. Pickwick, I told you all about that. Oh, love. Was this out near the Yacht Basin where you played? Oh, yeah. It was right across the- West End? No, that's the way you go on the West End, but we get to West…

33.t: Four years at the Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's Tea Room
33.s: He explains how he persuaded Mr. Cobb to open the tea room, drew his own following and effectively ran the place without a contract.
33.ch: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
33.q: Four years in Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's, Cobb's Tea Room. Eleven to one at night. We didn't get six sets in. We'd get a beer and get three sets and the night's over. And then when we had competitions with the other places trying to put us out of business, they brought in acts. And Mr.…

248.t: O'Neal Lavishay and the Fuqua hall off Basin Street
248.s: Dawson recalls violinist O'Neal Lavishay and the nightclub hall run by George Fuqua, with the layout and clientele.
248.q: O'Neal Lavishay, well he was a violin player, I worked with him at a few clothes, it's been a little while. He died. He was a violin player. He worked for, he was, he worked for the post office too, he's a mail carrier. And he played violin, he played over at a few clothes, had a fella called a few…

724.t: Small groups and the low-down tunks he avoided
724.s: Allen asks about tunks and trio work; Burbank never went into the rough places (text heavily garbled).
724.q: Oakland What about these tunks? Did you ever go into the tunks and play there? No. Did you ever hear any clarinet plays in the tunks? The real rarity guys? I don't remember, no. In fact, you said tunk. Now what do you mean by tunk? I mean a real low-round place where they would just maybe have a…

663.t: Playing Jackson Square and the Dream Castle
663.s: He has played Jackson Square for fifteen or sixteen years and played at the Dream Castle; mentions his stolen steel guitar and a gift guitar.
663.q: Blue. Alright. And the Dream Castle. And uh. I thought. Yeah. My boy. Right now. I'm looking for him mostly anytime. Come into this store. He brought my little guitar that's stolen you know. And I know that.

773.t: Rugello and the nightclubs where Arnold played
773.s: A saxophonist who lived on Prayer, and nightclubs: the bungalow, roadhouse, Cadillac and Lannasa's place.
773.q: Oh, yeah. Sure. He was a little saxophone player. Saxophone, kind of thing. Oh, yeah. And I think he used to be a whole lot with D.D.

266.t: Clubs along Canal Boulevard and neighbors who lived there
266.s: Jones maps the clubs near Lenfance (Muffins, Wishing Well, Starlight Inn) and names local musicians who lived there.
266.q: Okay, there was a place called Sam Sires. The Starlight Inn. The Starbright Inn. Starlight Inn. On the same side of the railroad track, right? See, there were four places.

268.t: Going back to La Vida with Handy, about eight years
268.s: After the Entertainers he joined Handy at La Vida. Several band changes and a switch to a nightclub marked the roughly eight years there.
268.ch: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
268.q: I see. Did Handy take over the job, you think? Yes, Handy, I think, uh, Handy comes after Paul, I think. I see. I just wondered if they had a humbug, if he got sick, or what? See, at the time they had, uh, I think, uh, she was playing trumpet then. I think Isaiah Morgan was playing trumpet at that…

272.t: Joining Buzzy Williams at the Slipper, October 1928
272.s: A union magazine puts him at Morrison's in May 1928 and with Buzzy Williams at the Slipper that October; Lizana calls it a nice little place.
272.ch: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
272.q: Yeah. Just like the other night there, I said, yeah, no, I'm alive about three weeks ago. Mm-hmm. I get a letter in the mail, and I open it. And it's been so long since I've seen the boy, I didn't remember his name. Jake can't tell me who he was. Mm-hmm. And somebody sends me a letter, and…

275.s: He clarifies where he played the Chanticleer and Tradewinds; the tape ends on a gambling club question.
275.q: The Chanticleer is in Baltimore. And I played it to Tradewinds in Washington, D.C. And a Chanticleer in Washington, D.C. at 14th and K.

628.t: Nightly jobs and the day work around them
628.s: Williams tells of playing most nights, including at the Marcelloan on Charters Street, the Fifth Ward Athletic Club and Shadowland, with trumpeters Rickard Lexkin and Herman Franklin.
628.q: played music back in those times? I used to like the wood. Loved the wood. Drive, truck, drive, truck, and sometimes I'd get on a job and play every night. I played at the Marcelloan on Charter Street until they come in with a big doobie. They come in with a big doobie. I don't know that place.…

152.t: The Dew Drop's rooms and owner Frank Pannier
152.s: He describes the front and back rooms and Frank Pannier, who owned the club and hotel and treated him well.
152.ch: Dew Drop and the name Red
152.q: Oh yeah. Mm-hmm. The stage was bigger. Uh, in the front, the, the bar was around the, the bandstand. Uh, the, the, the show was up there and the bar was like a, a U. Right, a horseshoe. Yeah, a horseshoe.

432.s: He played a trio job there and recalls Creole Fiesta work.
432.q: No, well I played with a little trio over there at Robinson and Houston Avenue for a while there. Well I had oil on piano and I had a boy playing drums, I can't think of his name. You're on my lap, huh? Yeah I had oil on piano and I had another boy sing, play a great trumpet. No he sang, he played…

664.t: The Brunies halfway house as an early nightclub
664.s: He locates the halfway house, calls it one of the first New Orleans nightclubs, and says Abbey's band was strictly Dixieland.
664.q: I don't know what they got there now. I think it's torn down. They had to tear down and come through there with that street. Yeah. They made that overpass there and that underpass. Uh-huh. You know where the new basin was. Yeah I know where it is. Right where the new bridge used to go over the new…

283.t: Hotel rooms and nightclubs: the Cave
283.s: He describes a hotel nightclub on Baronne Street and The Cave with its big revues.
283.ch: Reel two to four: pay, tailgate and style
283.q: Well, they used to have big reviews, like Rainey Young from Chicago, New York, you know. They'd bring about 15 gallons and big shows, like Singers and Acrobatic and everything, you know. But it was a beautiful place down there.

572.t: Kid Rena's drummer and Kid Punch
572.s: They recall Chani and Kid Punch, and clubs such as the Pelican and Sam Morgan's.
572.ch: Reading, repertoire and New Orleans players
572.q: Kid Punch... Kid Punch played wonderful. Played wonderful plenty. He used to play Pelican Club on all... Mm-hmm. On South Ramp off street. Yeah. Then later on I saw him on Chicago and all.

176.s: They list the clubs on Decatur Street where they worked, including Popeye's, the Kingfish and a Filipino place.
176.q: Well, I was working at the Kingfish when I met you. Yeah. When I met you. And before that? Well, I was at the Rialto nightclub. And I wait for... When did Popeye's come in? Well, I worked at Popeye right there on Decatur Street. We worked there together. We worked at Popeye right there on Decatur…

289.t: Club policies, decor and the streetcar gimmick
289.s: The club had music five nights a week, no cover, glass-brick decor, and the Claiborne streetcar conductor announced it, filling the place beyond capacity.
289.q: No, yeah, five, yeah, five nights a week. We changed by five nights. We was open, we never did close. We opened from, uh,

602.t: French Quarter bands Gabriel booked, Tony Pesina and the Johnsons
602.s: He was the first Black band in the French Quarter, booked bands for clubs, and started Tucker Cole and Laverne Smith.
602.q: Some of them did it. When they come to Elmore, Elmore told them I'd be damned if I'm doing it. And she tried for her doing this to get it done. Uh-huh. But they wouldn't do it at our place. The doghouse had it for a while. And, uh, Puffy House and them had shoes there. They had a little place,…

830.t: Places little George played: cabarets, Franklin Street and Jackson Avenue
830.s: Charlotte recalls where little George played in the 1920s, including a Jackson Avenue place with Steve Lewis where his gold watch was stolen.
830.q: What's some places you remember where Lil' George played at? Other than the music box when he was on that Jitney job. I know he stayed there a few years.

84.t: First saxophone job at the Entertainers Cafe
84.s: He played his first sax job at the Entertainers Cafe on Basin Street, which ran from the mid-1920s into the 1930s.
84.q: Yeah, he's the first one that showed me how to finger saxophone. From then on, I had, like I said, I had it on three weeks and I would play my first job. And there was no set up either because I would play it at the Entertainer's Cavalry. All the musicians come. All Creed and all Colour went there.…

782.t: Red Garter band changes and George Lewis's group
782.s: George Lewis takes over the Red Garter, with a modern-sounding earlier band, a weak pianist and a better-sounding room.
782.ch: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
782.q: Well, the Red Garter. Yeah, I heard the stuff there. I've been there when I went to the Sunday afternoon. And I was calling for girls to play. And now when yours, Lewis.

118.t: Sporty Johnson and the Club Desire
118.s: Williams knew Sporty Johnson; Club Desire booked big acts and hired local small players like him.
118.q: It was beautiful. They brought all big attractions in Club Desire. You remember when the Fat Davin new first mate B? He was strong, going big. Well, they kept him at Club Desire. Rod Brown, that was a big man. Remember that big number that stands out today? What's that? That big number is Good…

302.s: He lists clubs he played, including the Robin Hood, Rhythm Club with Joe Robichaux, the Famous Door, Dreamland and Absinthe House.
302.q: When I was with Dave Tholomew, I played at the Robin Hood, and we played up at the, what's the name of this club up on Eagle Street. We stayed up there quite a while. At the Gravestone.

177.t: Playing with Burbank and Moran uptown and at the Dandy Inn
177.s: Jiles recalls the Burbank band with Moran, Talbidge and Lester Lewis, the nights at Messmer's near the Dandy Inn, and an uptown spot they cannot name.
177.q: Well it was, I think it was Albert Boybank. Must have been. Yeah it was, with Albert Boybank. That's right, yeah. That's right. And Moran, that's right. That's right. That's where Moran the trumpet player.

952.t: Plans for a nightclub in Jefferson Parish
952.s: Pete says he considered new locations after a lease fight on Bourbon Street and might build a bigger place.
952.q: talking about that uh a few years uh a few years ago when i was fighting with my lease uh in my building on bourbon street yeah but since then i bought a new car uh club in a 200 block which i uh we've been having for about a year and a half and then uh but we were seriously thinking about moving…

127.t: Lights in clubs, Preservation Hall travels and the dark 25
127.s: Asked about flashing lights, Punch says the darkest place he knew was the 25.
127.q: No, no. The darkest place I went in here was way back there at 25 when I went in... at 25 where Lewiston was from. You could dark, damn light. You could hardly see it there. Well, that darkest place I don't remember.

101.t: The Club Riviera and Jordan Chambers
101.s: Chambers's club was the Black counterpart of the Plantation; Mother Tough's sessions.
101.q: Jordan Chambers was a – for some – I don’t know how he gained his wealth, but he was a pretty wealthy guy. He was a political person. He bought this club out on [North] Sarah [Street] and [East] Finney [Avenue], I think it was. I think it was on Sarah and Finney. It was a huge club, beautifully…
